docs.title: Use original benchmarks
docs.text: For benchmark comparisons, obtain original data from its documented publisher or a framework's official dataset loader. Preserve the original train/test split, license, preprocessing and attribution. Installing the datasets extra adds scikit-learn; it does not turn every synthetic loader into an original-data loader.

docs.title: Formula catalog
docs.text:
Generated from the repository by python scripts/generate_reference.py.

285 formulas across 10 domains.

Every name below is available through MathForge().get(name). Formulas are symbolic building blocks; check their assumptions and input domains before interpreting a result. A symbolic optimization step is separate from a model optimizer, and symbolic metric expressions are separate from the batch evaluation API.

from neurogebra import MathForge

expression = MathForge().get("swish")
print(expression.symbolic_expr)
print(expression.params)
print(expression.gradient("x").symbolic_expr)

docs.title: Release Notes & Changelog
docs.text:
Current source target: v3.0.0, prepared 2026-11-25.

Read the 3.0.0 release notes, migration guide, and technical review. Hosted publication is performed separately by the maintainer.

docs.title: v2.8.3 — Cross-Platform Python 3.9 Compatibility & Docs Overhaul
docs.text:
• Restored full Python 3.9 runtime compatibility across Linux (ubuntu-22.04), Windows, and macOS CI runners by converting PEP 604 runtime union type hints (|) to PEP 563 (from __future__ import annotations) and typing.Optional.
  • Organized documentation with a PyTorch-style hierarchy, NeuroGebra logo teal (#008484), black (#0A0B0B), and white (#FFFFFF) design system, full API coverage, and up-to-date tutorials for all v2.8 subsystems.

docs.title: v2.8.2 — Rich LaTeX Rendering & Mathematical Audit Hardening (V01–V20)
docs.text:
• Rich LaTeX Math Rendering: Added _repr_latex_(), latex(), and to_latex() on Expression plus rich display(Math(...)) outputs in Project 13 Notebook.
  • Optimizer Integration (V01): Model.compile accepts standalone Optimizer instances (SGD, Adam, RMSprop) and string "rmsprop", stepped via LayerParam wrappers.
  • Scheduler Stepping (V02): Guaranteed epoch-end stepping in both Model.fit and EducationalTrainer.train.
  • Exact LayerNorm VJP (V03): Feature-scaled analytical backward pass verified against numerical finite differences.
  • PINN Multi-Parameter Gradients (V04): Differential equation residual loss differentiates both weights and biases.
  • Complete Serialization & Optimizer Moments (V05): Model.save() and Model.load() persist ResidualDense weights/skips, LayerNorm parameters, running statistics, step counters, and initialize moment buffers cleanly.
  • Numerical & Autograd Hardening (V06–V15): Macro F1 per-class averaging, leaf gradient accumulation preservation, negative-axis Tensor.transpose normalization, Softmax underflow stability, sample-weighted batch metrics, asymmetric even-kernel Conv2D same-padding, modern bridge layers (LayerNorm, GlobalAveragePooling2D, ResidualDense), and Softplus / Box-Cox stability.

docs.title: v2.8.1 — Enterprise Emoji Elimination & Hardened CI Matrix
docs.text:
• Eliminated all emoji characters across code, docstrings, markdown documentation, examples, and configurations.
  • Modernized CI workflows across Ubuntu, Windows, and Apple Silicon macOS runners for Python 3.9–3.12.

docs.title: v2.8.0 — SciML, Schedulers, Zero-Dep Metrics, Modern Layers & 20 GPU Notebooks
docs.text:
• Introduced neurogebra.science.PINN for differential equation solving.
  • Introduced neurogebra.optim standalone optimizers (SGD, Adam, RMSprop) and LR schedulers (StepLR, CosineAnnealingLR, ExponentialLR, ReduceLROnPlateau).
  • Introduced neurogebra.metrics (12 classification and regression evaluation functions with zero extra dependencies).
  • Added LayerNorm, GlobalAveragePooling2D, ResidualDense, and Model.add() chaining to ModelBuilder.
  • Authored and executed 20 GPU notebook projects (examples/projects/01–20).

docs.title: v2.6.0 – v2.7.0 — Native C-JIT & CUDA GPU Engine + 48 Datasets
docs.text:
• Added neurogebra.acceleration compiling symbolic expressions dynamically into AVX2 SIMD C++ shared objects (up to 2.04x speedup) and NVIDIA CUDA kernels via NVRTC (up to 4.76x speedup on RTX 5070).
  • Expanded built-in dataset catalog to 48 loaders across Datasets, ExpandedDatasets, and CombinedDatasets.
  • Added Model.load(), Model.train_on_batch(), full BatchNorm VJP, and public neurogebra.bridges exports (to_pytorch, model_to_pytorch, to_tensorflow, model_to_tensorflow, to_jax).

docs.text:
pip install --upgrade neurogebra
  • PyPI Project: neurogebra
  • Full Changelog: CHANGELOG.md on GitHub

docs.title: NeuroGebra 3.0.0
docs.text:
Release: 3.0.0 · Published November 2026.

NeuroGebra 3.0 makes the library easier to explore and fixes important edge cases in training, checkpointing and scientific experiments. The documentation now presents one coherent guide from an executable formula to an inspectable model.

docs.title: Highlights & Interactive Web Experience
docs.text:
• Interactive Documentation: Interactive formula explorer, activation visualization, and loss progression demo right on the home page with full accessibility and keyboard navigation support.
  • Granular API Documentation: Dedicated reference guides for Expression, MathForge, Value, Tensor, Trainer, and NeuroCraft with complete signatures, parameters, and executable examples.
  • Classic Documentation Design: Warm paper tones, teal accents, serif headings, light/dark themes, responsive navigation, and local system fonts.
  • Full Reference Catalogs: Generated catalogs covering all 285 formulas and 48 dataset loaders, with return conventions and provenance.
  • Frontend Quality Assurance: Automated regression tests (tests/web/home-demo.test.cjs) validating graph bounds, ARIA states, and UI/Python agreement.
  • Updated Guides: Architecture guide, first program, capability matrix, troubleshooting, contributor guide, migration notes and technical review.

docs.title: Runtime & Engine Fixes
docs.text:
• Optimizer State Persistence: Preserve built-in Adam, SGD, and RMSprop configuration, step counters, and momentum/velocity buffers in model checkpoints.
  • Numerically Stable Softmax / Cross-Entropy: Compute Dense softmax cross-entropy loss directly from logits, with exact fused gradients for class indices and probability targets.
  • Categorical Target Validation: Validate integer categorical labels and probability distributions; preserve true general softmax vector-Jacobian product.
  • PINN Residual Derivatives: Differentiate every residual weight and bias (supporting matrices with >256 entries), normalize multi-output gradients across all elements, and safely restore parameters upon callback exceptions.
  • Analytical Derivative Caching: Cache and reuse analytical derivative expressions and compiled numerical functions across training epochs.
  • Portable Native Acceleration: Safe C compiler target detection, compiler-aware cache hashing, and configurable cache root via NEUROGEBRA_CACHE_DIR.
  • Checkpointing Hygiene: Respect metrics=[] and explicitly reject unsupported custom optimizer checkpoint serialization.

docs.title: Upgrade notes
docs.text: The migration guide explains numerical behavior changes, old checkpoints and native backend compatibility. The core package still requires Python 3.9+. No claim of universal performance superiority over other ML frameworks is made in this release.

docs.title: Known boundaries
docs.text: Neural models and PINNs train with NumPy. PINN residual differentiation is numerical and can be expensive. The CUDA path evaluates supported expressions and transfers host arrays per call. Framework bridge capabilities differ. Pickle checkpoints require trusted inputs, and scheduler/RNG state is not saved. See capabilities and the review and roadmap.

docs.title: Validate this checkout
docs.text:
python -m pytest tests -q
node --test tests/web/home-demo.test.cjs
python -m mkdocs build --strict
python scripts/check_docs.py --site site
python scripts/check_release.py --tag v3.0.0
python -m build
python -m twine check dist/*

Use Python 3.11+ for check_release.py. See publishing instructions for the maintainer release sequence.

docs.title: Migrate from 2.x to 3.0
docs.text:
Most core imports remain the same. This major release deliberately changes some numerical edge cases and native compilation defaults. Re-run your experiment's correctness checks before comparing results across versions.

Area 2.x behavior 3.0 behavior / action Dense softmax + categorical cross-entropy Clipped probability loss could report about 27.63 for a wrong-class logit gap of 2000 Stable logits loss reports 2000; gradients follow the actual objective. Expect different loss curves at saturation Sparse labels Fractional values could be truncated to integers Invalid/fractional labels raise ValueError; provide integer class IDs Probability targets Invalid distributions could be accepted Provide finite nonnegative rows summing to one PINN residual gradients Larger weight matrices could crash; gradients were silently sampled Every parameter is differentiated. Larger models may take longer but no weights are silently omitted Multi-output PINNs Data gradients were over-scaled by output width Mean-squared-error gradients normalize over every output element Residual callbacks An internal TypeError could trigger a second call with a different signature Internal exceptions propagate, and perturbed parameters are restored Model checkpoints Architecture/weights loaded with fresh optimizer buffers New checkpoints restore built-in optimizer configuration, step and buffers Old checkpoints No saved optimizer snapshot Valid older checkpoints load with fresh optimizer state; files that never saved complete layer weights cannot reconstruct the missing parameters Custom optimizers State could be silently lost when saving save() rejects unsupported optimizer types explicitly Metric selection metrics=[] became the default accuracy list Empty selection remains empty Native C target -mavx2 was forced on many x86 systems Portable compiler target; rebenchmark native kernels on your machine C options and variables Arbitrary optimization string / incomplete variable list Supported -O* values and complete unique variables are validated

docs.title: Install from this checkout
docs.text:
python -m pip install -e .
python -c "import neurogebra; print(neurogebra.__version__)"

After publication, pin a deployment with python -m pip install "neurogebra==3.0.0".

docs.title: Check a model checkpoint
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from neurogebra import Model

# Load only your own or otherwise trusted pickle checkpoint.
restored = Model.load("model.pkl")
# Compare against predictions recorded before the upgrade.

Scheduler state, data order and RNG state are not serialized. Capture those separately for a reproducible experiment. Model bridges need their own prediction/gradient checks after conversion.

Read the release notes for the full scope and capabilities for the remaining boundaries.

docs.title: Science and speed
docs.text:
Move from an inspectable experiment toward a measured result. These guides cover native expression execution, educational scientific computing, optimization and evaluation.

Guide What it covers Native expression acceleration C/CUDA setup, compilation, precision, cache and hardware boundaries Physics-informed neural networks Data and equation residuals, finite differences, oscillator and Burgers examples Optimizers and schedules SGD, Adam, RMSprop and learning-rate policies Evaluation metrics Classification and regression metrics with NumPy Regularization Penalties and model complexity Performance engineering Fair benchmarks, bottlenecks and an execution-backend roadmap Framework bridges Supported adapters and conversion limits Custom expressions Extend the symbolic building blocks

Neural models and PINNs train with NumPy. Native acceleration is scoped to supported expression kernels; read the capability matrix before choosing a backend.

docs.title: Native expression acceleration
docs.text: Compile supported symbolic expressions to native C shared libraries or NVIDIA CUDA kernels. These backends apply to expression evaluation; neural-model and PINN training remain NumPy based.

docs.title: Inspect the environment
docs.text:
from neurogebra import get_acceleration_info
print(get_acceleration_info())

The result includes c_jit_available, c_compiler, cuda_available, cuda_device and cuda_compute_capability. Treat availability as a starting check; validate the actual expression on the target machine.

docs.title: Compile an expression
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from neurogebra import Expression, is_c_available

expr = Expression("energy", "0.5 * m * v**2", params={"m": 2.0})
v = np.linspace(0.0, 10.0, 1000)
baseline = expr.eval(v=v, backend="numpy")

if is_c_available():
    expr.compile(backend="c")
    native = expr.eval(v=v, backend="c")
    np.testing.assert_allclose(native, baseline)

docs.title: Backend boundaries
docs.text:
Backend Precision Requirements Current behavior numpy Usually float64 Core installation Vectorized SymPy-generated NumPy callable c float64 GCC/Clang toolchain, writable cache Portable native kernel, NumPy broadcasting, disk cache cuda float32 NVIDIA device/driver, NVRTC, compatible CUDA Python bindings NVRTC compilation and device launch; host arrays copied for each call

3.0 uses the compiler's portable CPU target. A compiler accepting -mavx2 does not establish that a CPU can execute AVX2; the previous forced flag was unsafe on older x86 machines. Compiler identity is now included in the C cache key.

The fast extra installs Numba but does not select a Numba backend. MSVC is not detected by the current compiler search, which looks for clang++, g++, gcc and clang.

docs.title: Low-level functions
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from neurogebra.acceleration import compile_c, is_c_available

if is_c_available():
    fn = compile_c("x*x + y", variables=["x", "y"], opt_level="-O3")
    out = fn(np.array([1.0, 2.0]), 3.0)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(out, [4.0, 7.0])

import numpy as np
from neurogebra.acceleration import compile_cuda, is_cuda_available

if is_cuda_available():
    fn = compile_cuda("x*x + 1", variables=["x"])
    x = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 1000, dtype=np.float32)
    out = fn(x)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(out, x*x + 1, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-6)

Supported C optimization arguments are -O0, -O1, -O2, -O3 and -Os. Variables must be unique and cover all free symbols. Unsupported symbolic constructs can fail at code generation or compilation; use the NumPy backend where appropriate.

docs.title: Cache and deployment
docs.text:
C artifacts are stored under ~/.neurogebra/cache/c_jit by default. Set NEUROGEBRA_CACHE_DIR to use another root; artifacts use its c_jit subdirectory. Treat compiled artifacts as local build products rather than portable wheels. Avoid concurrent processes building the same cold cache entry; atomic multi-process cache coordination is a future improvement.

CUDA context/module lifetime and broader driver-version coverage need further validation. Run native tests on the target hardware before deploying an accelerated workload.

docs.title: Benchmark responsibly
docs.text: Historical kernel speedup figures are workload-specific and are not a validated 3.0 end-to-end training comparison. Use the performance guide to reproduce timings with matched precision, input size, compilation, transfer boundaries and output tolerances.

docs.title: Zero-Dependency Evaluation Metrics
docs.text: neurogebra.metrics provides 12 standard classification and regression evaluation functions implemented purely in NumPy—requiring no scikit-learn runtime dependency.

docs.title: Classification Metrics
docs.text:
All classification metrics automatically decode integer class labels, one-hot probability matrices (N, C), and binary probability predictions (N,) / (N, 1) cleanly.

import numpy as np
from neurogebra.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    precision_score,
    recall_score,
    f1_score,
    confusion_matrix,
    classification_report,
)

y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2])
y_pred = np.array([0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 0])

print(f"Accuracy:    {accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred):.4f}")
print(f"Macro F1:    {f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='macro'):.4f}")
print(f"Weighted F1: {f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted'):.4f}")
print("Confusion Matrix:\n", confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred))
print("\n" + classification_report(y_true, y_pred, target_names=["Class A", "Class B", "Class C"]))

docs.title: Averaging Modes
docs.text: Function Supported average Modes Behavior precision_score "macro", "micro" Per-class precision mean (macro) or global TP / pred sum (micro) recall_score "macro", "micro" Per-class recall mean (macro) or global TP / support sum (micro) f1_score "macro", "micro", "weighted" Unweighted per-class F1 mean (macro), global micro F1, or support-weighted F1

docs.title: Regression Metrics
docs.text:
Regression metrics validate target shapes consistently and align 1D (N,) vectors with column matrices (N, 1) automatically.

import numpy as np
from neurogebra.metrics import (
    mean_squared_error,
    root_mean_squared_error,
    mean_absolute_error,
    mean_absolute_percentage_error,
    r2_score,
    explained_variance_score,
)

y_true = np.array([3.0, 5.0, 2.5, 7.0])
y_pred = np.array([[2.8], [5.1], [2.4], [7.2]])  # (N, 1) aligned automatically

print(f"MSE:  {mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred):.4f}")
print(f"RMSE: {root_mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred):.4f}")
print(f"MAE:  {mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred):.4f}")
print(f"MAPE: {mean_absolute_percentage_error(y_true, y_pred):.2f}%")
print(f"R2:   {r2_score(y_true, y_pred):.4f}")
print(f"EVS:  {explained_variance_score(y_true, y_pred):.4f}")

docs.title: Summary of Functions
docs.text: Metric Mathematical Formula Range / Ideal mean_squared_error \(\frac{1}{N}\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\) \([0, \infty)\), lower is better root_mean_squared_error \(\sqrt{\text{MSE}}\) \([0, \infty)\), same units as target mean_absolute_error \(\frac{1}{N}\sum \|y_i - \hat{y}_i\|\) \([0, \infty)\), robust to outliers mean_absolute_percentage_error \(\frac{100}{N}\sum \frac{\|y_i - \hat{y}_i\|}{\max(\|y_i\|, \epsilon)}\) Percentage error (\(\%\)) r2_score \(1 - \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}\) \((-\infty, 1]\), 1.0 optimal explained_variance_score \(1 - \frac{\text{Var}(y - \hat{y})}{\text{Var}(y)}\) \((-\infty, 1]\), 1.0 optimal

docs.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN)
docs.text: neurogebra.science.PINN provides a pure-Python/NumPy solver for Ordinary and Partial Differential Equations (ODEs and PDEs). Rather than fitting data points alone, a PINN embeds known differential conservation laws directly into the training loss.

docs.title: Mathematical Formulation
docs.text:
Given initial/boundary observations \(\{(\mathbf{x}_d^{(i)}, u_d^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{N_d}\) and interior collocation coordinates \(\{\mathbf{x}_c^{(j)}\}_{j=1}^{N_c}\), the network minimizes the composite physics objective:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}}(\theta) + \lambda_{\text{PDE}} \, \mathcal{L}_{\text{residual}}(\theta)\]

where:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{data}} = \frac{1}{N_d} \sum_{i=1}^{N_d} \left(u_\theta(\mathbf{x}_d^{(i)}) - u_d^{(i)}\right)^2, \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{residual}} = \frac{1}{N_c} \sum_{j=1}^{N_c} \left| \mathcal{R}[u_\theta](\mathbf{x}_c^{(j)}) \right|^2\]

All required spatial and temporal derivatives (\(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_k}, \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_k^2}\)) are computed directly via central finite differences, and both weights and biases receive gradient updates through Adam optimization.

Educational solver and computational cost

Residual parameter gradients also use central finite differences: two residual evaluations per weight or bias, per step. Version 3.0 differentiates every parameter. Start with small networks and collocation grids; this implementation is not a GPU/autograd PDE solver. Check residual and boundary errors against a known solution before drawing scientific conclusions.

docs.title: Quick Start: 1D Damped Harmonic Oscillator (ODE)
docs.text:
Solve \(m \frac{d^2 u}{dt^2} + c \frac{du}{dt} + k u = 0\) with initial displacement conditions:

import numpy as np
from neurogebra.science import PINN

# A small network for an API walkthrough; increase only after validation.
pinn = PINN(layer_sizes=[1, 8, 1], activation="tanh", seed=42)

# Boundary / initial condition points
t_data = np.array([[0.0], [0.05]])
u_data = np.array([[1.0], [0.98]])

# Interior domain collocation grid
t_colloc = np.linspace(0.0, 4.0, 16).reshape(-1, 1)

# Train using the built-in harmonic oscillator residual
history = pinn.fit(
    X_data=t_data,
    y_data=u_data,
    X_colloc=t_colloc,
    residual_fn=pinn.harmonic_oscillator_residual,
    epochs=20,
    lr=0.01,
    lambda_pde=1.0,
)

u_pred = pinn.predict(t_colloc)

This short run demonstrates the API; it is not a convergence guarantee. The two early-time observations approximate initial behavior rather than imposing an exact initial-velocity constraint.

docs.title: Solving 1D Viscous Burgers' Equation (PDE)
docs.text:
Enforce nonlinear fluid dynamics conservation across \((x, t) \in [-1, 1] \times [0, 1]\):

\[\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + u \frac{\partial u}{\partial x} - \nu \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} = 0\] 
import numpy as np
from neurogebra.science import PINN

pinn = PINN(layer_sizes=[2, 8, 1], activation="tanh", seed=7)

# Boundary & initial data (e.g., u(x, 0) = -sin(pi * x), u(+-1, t) = 0)
x0 = np.linspace(-1, 1, 40)
ic_coords = np.column_stack([x0, np.zeros_like(x0)])
ic_vals = (-np.sin(np.pi * x0)).reshape(-1, 1)

tb = np.linspace(0, 1, 20)
bc_left = np.column_stack([-np.ones_like(tb), tb])
bc_right = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(tb), tb])
X_data = np.vstack([ic_coords, bc_left, bc_right])
y_data = np.vstack([ic_vals, np.zeros((40, 1))])

# Interior spacetime collocation grid [x, t]
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
X_colloc = np.column_stack([
    rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0, 24),
    rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0, 24),
])

history = pinn.fit(
    X_data=X_data,
    y_data=y_data,
    X_colloc=X_colloc,
    residual_fn=lambda net, pts: net.burgers_residual(pts, nu=0.01 / np.pi),
    epochs=20,
    lr=0.008,
    lambda_pde=0.5,
)

docs.title: Defining Custom Physical Residuals
docs.text:
Write any ODE or PDE residual callable taking (pinn, X_colloc) (or bound method residual_fn(X_colloc)) and computing derivatives with pinn.compute_gradient and pinn.compute_second_derivative:

import numpy as np
from neurogebra.science import PINN

def heat_equation_residual(net: PINN, coords: np.ndarray, alpha: float = 0.25) -> np.ndarray:
    """Enforce 1D Heat PDE: du/dt - alpha * d^2u/dx^2 = 0 on coords [x, t]."""
    u_t = net.compute_gradient(coords, var_idx=1)
    u_xx = net.compute_second_derivative(coords, var_idx=0)
    return u_t - alpha * u_xx

docs.title: Supported Activations for Smooth Physics Fields
docs.text:
Smooth infinite-order differentiable activations avoid piecewise derivative artifacts when optimizing second-order PDE residuals:

Activation Behavior Best Suited For "tanh" (Default) Bounded smooth \(C^\infty\) Boundary-value PDEs, Burgers' equation "sin" Periodic / SIREN-style derivatives Oscillatory waves, Helmholtz equations "gelu" Smooth Gaussian-gated Coupled multi-scale physics fields "relu" Piecewise linear Non-smooth baseline comparison only

docs.title: Activation Functions
docs.text: Activation functions are the secret sauce that gives neural networks the power to learn complex patterns.

docs.title: Why Activation Functions?
docs.text:
Without activation functions, a neural network is just a chain of linear transformations — which collapses into a single linear function. Activation functions add non-linearity, allowing networks to learn curves, boundaries, and complex relationships.

Without activation: Layer1(Layer2(x)) = W1*(W2*x + b2) + b1 = W*x + b  (still linear!)
With activation:    relu(W1 * relu(W2*x + b2) + b1)  → Can learn ANY function!

docs.title: Exploring Activations in Neurogebra
docs.text:
from neurogebra import MathForge

forge = MathForge()

# List all activation functions
activations = forge.list_all(category="activation")
print(activations)
# ['relu', 'sigmoid', 'tanh', 'leaky_relu', 'swish', 'gelu', 'softplus', ...]

docs.title: ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit)
docs.text:
The most popular activation function in deep learning.

\[f(x) = \max(0, x)\] 
relu = forge.get("relu")

# Formula
print(relu.symbolic_expr)  # Max(0, x)

# Behavior
print(relu.eval(x=5))    # 5   (positive → pass through)
print(relu.eval(x=-3))   # 0   (negative → blocked)
print(relu.eval(x=0))    # 0   (zero → zero)

# Metadata
print(relu.metadata["description"])
# "Rectified Linear Unit - outputs x if x > 0, else 0"
print(relu.metadata["pros"])
# ['Fast computation', 'No vanishing gradient for positive values']
print(relu.metadata["cons"])
# ['Dead neurons for negative values', 'Not zero-centered']

When to use ReLU

Default choice for hidden layers. Use it unless you have a specific reason not to.

docs.title: Sigmoid
docs.text:
Maps any real number to a value between 0 and 1.

\[f(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}\] 
sigmoid = forge.get("sigmoid")

print(sigmoid.eval(x=0))      # 0.5  (center)
print(sigmoid.eval(x=10))     # ≈ 1.0 (large positive → 1)
print(sigmoid.eval(x=-10))    # ≈ 0.0 (large negative → 0)

When to use Sigmoid

Output layer for binary classification (yes/no, spam/not-spam). Outputs a probability.

docs.title: Tanh (Hyperbolic Tangent)
docs.text:
Like Sigmoid, but outputs between -1 and 1.

\[f(x) = \tanh(x) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}\] 
tanh = forge.get("tanh")

print(tanh.eval(x=0))     # 0.0  (zero-centered!)
print(tanh.eval(x=5))     # ≈ 1.0
print(tanh.eval(x=-5))    # ≈ -1.0

When to use Tanh

Hidden layers when zero-centered output matters (e.g., RNNs, LSTMs).

docs.title: Leaky ReLU
docs.text:
ReLU but allows a small gradient for negative values.

\[f(x) = \max(\alpha x, x) \quad \text{where } \alpha = 0.01\] 
leaky = forge.get("leaky_relu")

print(leaky.eval(x=5))    # 5
print(leaky.eval(x=-5))   # -0.05  (not zero! Small leak)

# Custom alpha
leaky02 = forge.get("leaky_relu", params={"alpha": 0.2})
print(leaky02.eval(x=-5))  # -1.0 (bigger leak)

When to use Leaky ReLU

When you're worried about "dead neurons" (neurons that always output 0 with standard ReLU).

docs.title: Swish (SiLU)
docs.text:
Self-gated activation — often outperforms ReLU.

\[f(x) = x \cdot \sigma(x) = \frac{x}{1 + e^{-x}}\] 
swish = forge.get("swish")

print(swish.eval(x=5))    # ≈ 4.97
print(swish.eval(x=-5))   # ≈ -0.03
print(swish.eval(x=0))    # 0.0

When to use Swish

Modern deep networks. Found by Google's AutoML to outperform ReLU in many cases.

docs.title: GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit)
docs.text:
The activation used in GPT, BERT, and modern Transformers.

\[f(x) = 0.5x\left(1 + \tanh\left(\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(x + 0.044715x^3\right)\right)\right)\] 
gelu = forge.get("gelu")

print(gelu.eval(x=1))     # ≈ 0.841
print(gelu.eval(x=-1))    # ≈ -0.159
print(gelu.eval(x=0))     # 0.0

When to use GELU

Transformer models (BERT, GPT, ViT). The current state-of-the-art choice.

docs.title: Softplus
docs.text:
A smooth approximation of ReLU.

\[f(x) = \ln(1 + e^x)\] 
softplus = forge.get("softplus")

print(softplus.eval(x=5))    # ≈ 5.007
print(softplus.eval(x=-5))   # ≈ 0.007
print(softplus.eval(x=0))    # ≈ 0.693

docs.title: Comparison Table
docs.text: Activation Formula Range Best For ReLU \(\max(0, x)\) \([0, \infty)\) Default for hidden layers Sigmoid \(\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\) \((0, 1)\) Binary classification output Tanh \(\tanh(x)\) \((-1, 1)\) RNNs, zero-centered needs Leaky ReLU \(\max(\alpha x, x)\) \((-\infty, \infty)\) Preventing dead neurons Swish \(x \cdot \sigma(x)\) \((-\infty, \infty)\) Modern deep networks GELU see above \((-\infty, \infty)\) Transformers (BERT, GPT) Softplus \(\ln(1+e^x)\) \((0, \infty)\) Smooth ReLU alternative

docs.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
docs.text:
from neurogebra import MathForge
import numpy as np

forge = MathForge()

x = 1.0
print(f"{'Activation':>12} | f({x})")
print("-" * 30)

for name in ["relu", "sigmoid", "tanh", "leaky_relu", "swish", "gelu", "softplus"]:
    expr = forge.get(name)
    val = expr.eval(x=x)
    print(f"{name:>12} | {val:.4f}")

Output: 

  Activation | f(1.0)
------------------------------
        relu | 1.0000
     sigmoid | 0.7311
        tanh | 0.7616
  leaky_relu | 1.0000
       swish | 0.7311
        gelu | 0.8412
    softplus | 1.3133

docs.title: Gradients of Activation Functions
docs.text:
Understanding how gradients flow through activation functions is crucial:

for name in ["relu", "sigmoid", "tanh", "swish"]:
    expr = forge.get(name)
    grad = expr.gradient("x")

    print(f"{name}:")
    print(f"  f(x) = {expr.symbolic_expr}")
    print(f"  f'(x) = {grad.symbolic_expr}")
    print(f"  f'(1.0) = {grad.eval(x=1.0):.4f}")
    print()

docs.title: Try It Yourself!
docs.text:
Exercise

  1. Get all activation functions and evaluate them at x = -2, -1, 0, 1, 2
  2. Which activation outputs the largest value at x = 1?
  3. Which activation has the largest gradient at x = 0?
  4. Create a custom activation: f(x) = x * sigmoid(2*x)

docs.title: Autograd Engine
docs.text: Record a scalar computation and follow the derivative backward. Value provides an eager reverse-mode graph for small, inspectable calculations.

docs.title: A complete first example
docs.text:
from neurogebra.core.autograd import Value

x = Value(2.0)
y = x * x + 3 * x
y.backward()
print(y.data)  # 10.0
print(x.grad)  # 7.0

The derivative is 2*x + 3, so at x=2 it is 7. Reset leaf gradients between independent steps, rebuild the graph after parameter updates, and avoid changing a value between forward and backward. Continue with the Value reference or tensor guide.

docs.title: What is Autograd?
docs.text:
Autograd = Automatic Gradient computation.

Instead of computing derivatives by hand or symbolically, autograd:

  1. Records every operation you perform (builds a computation graph)
  2. When you call .backward(), it walks backwards through the graph
  3. Computes the gradient of each value using the chain rule

docs.title: The Value Class
docs.text:
Value wraps a number and tracks its gradient:

from neurogebra.core.autograd import Value

# Create values
a = Value(2.0)
b = Value(3.0)

print(a)  # Value(data=2.0, grad=0.0)
print(b)  # Value(data=3.0, grad=0.0)

docs.title: Forward Pass — Build the Graph
docs.text:
from neurogebra.core.autograd import Value

a = Value(2.0)
b = Value(3.0)

# Each operation creates a new Value and records the connection
c = a + b      # c = 5.0
d = a * b      # d = 6.0
e = c + d      # e = 11.0

print(f"a = {a.data}")  # 2.0
print(f"b = {b.data}")  # 3.0
print(f"c = a + b = {c.data}")  # 5.0
print(f"d = a * b = {d.data}")  # 6.0
print(f"e = c + d = {e.data}")  # 11.0

The computation graph looks like:

a (2.0) ──┬──[+]── c (5.0) ──┐
           │                   [+]── e (11.0)
b (3.0) ──┼──[+]── c         │
           │                   │
a (2.0) ──┤                   │
           └──[*]── d (6.0) ──┘
b (3.0) ──┘

docs.title: Backward Pass — Compute Gradients
docs.text:
# Compute de/da and de/db
e.backward()

print(f"de/da = {a.grad}")  # 4.0  (from + path: 1, from * path: b=3 → total: 1+3=4)
print(f"de/db = {b.grad}")  # 3.0  (from + path: 1, from * path: a=2 → total: 1+2=3)

Let's verify manually:

  • \(e = (a + b) + (a \cdot b) = a + b + ab\)
  • \(\frac{\partial e}{\partial a} = 1 + b = 1 + 3 = 4\)
  • \(\frac{\partial e}{\partial b} = 1 + a = 1 + 2 = 3\)

docs.title: Supported Operations
docs.text:
from neurogebra.core.autograd import Value

x = Value(2.0)

# Basic arithmetic
y = x + 3        # Addition
y = x * 3        # Multiplication
y = x ** 2       # Power
y = x - 1        # Subtraction
y = x / 2        # Division
y = -x           # Negation

# Activation functions
y = x.relu()     # ReLU
y = x.sigmoid()  # Sigmoid
y = x.tanh()     # Tanh
y = x.exp()      # Exponential
y = x.log()      # Natural log

docs.title: Building a Neuron
docs.text:
A single neuron is: \(output = activation(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b)\)

from neurogebra.core.autograd import Value

# Inputs
x1 = Value(2.0)
x2 = Value(3.0)

# Learnable parameters
w1 = Value(0.5)
w2 = Value(-0.3)
b = Value(0.1)

# Forward pass
z = w1 * x1 + w2 * x2 + b   # Linear: 0.5*2 + (-0.3)*3 + 0.1 = 0.2
output = z.sigmoid()          # Activation: σ(0.2) ≈ 0.5498

# Backward pass
output.backward()

print(f"Output: {output.data:.4f}")
print(f"Gradients:")
print(f"  dout/dw1 = {w1.grad:.4f}")
print(f"  dout/dw2 = {w2.grad:.4f}")
print(f"  dout/db  = {b.grad:.4f}")

docs.title: Manual Training Loop with Autograd
docs.text:
This is how PyTorch works internally — and now you can see every step:

from neurogebra.core.autograd import Value
import random

# Training data: y = 2x + 1
data = [(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7), (4, 9)]

# Learnable parameters
w = Value(0.0)
b = Value(0.0)
learning_rate = 0.01

for epoch in range(100):
    total_loss = Value(0.0)

    for x_val, y_val in data:
        # Forward pass
        x = Value(x_val)
        y_pred = w * x + b

        # Loss (MSE for one sample)
        loss = (y_pred - Value(y_val)) ** 2
        total_loss = total_loss + loss

    # Backward pass
    total_loss.backward()

    # Update parameters (gradient descent)
    w.data -= learning_rate * w.grad
    b.data -= learning_rate * b.grad

    # Reset gradients for next epoch
    w.grad = 0.0
    b.grad = 0.0

    if epoch % 20 == 0:
        print(f"Epoch {epoch:>3}: loss = {total_loss.data:.4f}, w = {w.data:.4f}, b = {b.data:.4f}")

print(f"\nLearned: y = {w.data:.2f}x + {b.data:.2f}")
# Expected: y ≈ 2.00x + 1.00

docs.title: Building a Mini Neural Network
docs.text:
from neurogebra.core.autograd import Value
import random

class Neuron:
    def __init__(self, n_inputs):
        self.w = [Value(random.uniform(-1, 1)) for _ in range(n_inputs)]
        self.b = Value(0.0)

    def __call__(self, x):
        # w · x + b
        act = sum((wi*xi for wi, xi in zip(self.w, x)), self.b)
        return act.relu()

    def parameters(self):
        return self.w + [self.b]

class MLP:
    def __init__(self, n_inputs, layer_sizes):
        sizes = [n_inputs] + layer_sizes
        self.layers = []
        for i in range(len(layer_sizes)):
            neurons = [Neuron(sizes[i]) for _ in range(sizes[i+1])]
            self.layers.append(neurons)

    def __call__(self, x):
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = [neuron(x) for neuron in layer]
        return x[0] if len(x) == 1 else x

    def parameters(self):
        return [p for layer in self.layers for neuron in layer for p in neuron.parameters()]

# Create a tiny network: 2 inputs → 4 hidden → 1 output
random.seed(42)
model = MLP(2, [4, 1])

print(f"Total parameters: {len(model.parameters())}")
# (2+1)*4 + (4+1)*1 = 12 + 5 = 17 parameters

docs.title: Zero Grad — Why It Matters
docs.text:
x = Value(3.0)
y = x ** 2
y.backward()
print(f"After first backward: x.grad = {x.grad}")  # 6.0

# If we compute again WITHOUT zeroing:
y = x ** 2
y.backward()
print(f"After second backward: x.grad = {x.grad}")  # 12.0 — WRONG! Accumulated!

# Always zero gradients between iterations:
x.zero_grad()
y = x ** 2
y.backward()
print(f"After zero + backward: x.grad = {x.grad}")  # 6.0 — Correct!

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Step What Happens Code Create values Wrap numbers x = Value(2.0) Forward pass Compute result y = w * x + b Backward pass Compute gradients y.backward() Read gradients See derivatives w.grad Update weights Learn w.data -= lr * w.grad Zero gradients Reset for next iteration w.zero_grad()

Next: Tensors →

docs.title: Expression Composition
docs.text: One of Neurogebra's most powerful features is the ability to combine simple expressions into complex ones.

docs.title: Why Compose?
docs.text:
Real ML involves complex math built from simple pieces:

  • Custom loss = MSE + regularization
  • Complex activation = combination of simple activations
  • Neural network layer = linear transformation + activation

docs.title: Addition
docs.text:
from neurogebra import MathForge

forge = MathForge()

mse = forge.get("mse")
mae = forge.get("mae")

# Combine losses
hybrid_loss = mse + mae
result = hybrid_loss.eval(y_pred=3.0, y_true=5.0)
print(f"Hybrid loss: {result}")  # MSE(4) + MAE(2) = 6

docs.title: Scalar Multiplication
docs.text:
# Weighted loss: 70% MSE + 30% MAE
weighted_loss = 0.7 * mse + 0.3 * mae

docs.title: String-Based Composition
docs.text:
# Quick composition from string
loss = forge.compose("mse + 0.1*mae")
print(loss.eval(y_pred=3.0, y_true=5.0))

docs.title: Functional Composition
docs.text:
Compose expressions like mathematical function composition: \(f(g(x))\)

from neurogebra import Expression, MathForge

forge = MathForge()

# Create a linear transformation
linear = Expression("linear", "2*x + 1")

# Compose with sigmoid: sigmoid(2*x + 1)
sigmoid = forge.get("sigmoid")
composed = sigmoid.compose(linear)

print(f"Formula: {composed.symbolic_expr}")

# Evaluate
print(f"f(0) = {composed.eval(x=0):.4f}")  # sigmoid(1) ≈ 0.7311
print(f"f(1) = {composed.eval(x=1):.4f}")  # sigmoid(3) ≈ 0.9526

docs.title: Building Custom Activations
docs.text:
from neurogebra import Expression, MathForge

forge = MathForge()

# Parametric ReLU: max(alpha*x, x)
prelu = Expression(
    "parametric_relu",
    "Max(alpha*x, x)",
    params={"alpha": 0.1},
    trainable_params=["alpha"],  # alpha can be learned!
    metadata={"category": "activation"}
)

print(prelu.eval(x=5))     # 5
print(prelu.eval(x=-5))    # -0.5 (with alpha=0.1)

# Register it for reuse
forge.register("prelu", prelu)

docs.title: Building Custom Loss Functions
docs.text:
# Focal Loss (used in object detection)
# It down-weights easy examples and focuses on hard ones
focal = Expression(
    "focal_loss",
    "-(alpha * y_true * (1-y_pred)**gamma * log(y_pred) + (1-alpha) * (1-y_true) * y_pred**gamma * log(1-y_pred))",
    params={"alpha": 0.25, "gamma": 2.0},
    metadata={
        "category": "loss",
        "description": "Focal loss for imbalanced classification"
    }
)

forge.register("focal_loss", focal)

docs.title: Building Regularized Losses
docs.text:
Regularization prevents overfitting by penalizing large weights:

from neurogebra import MathForge, Expression

forge = MathForge()

# Base loss
mse = forge.get("mse")

# L2 regularizer from repository
l2 = Expression("l2_term", "lambda_reg * w**2",
                params={"lambda_reg": 0.01})

# Regularized loss = MSE + L2
# In practice, you'd sum L2 over all weights
print("Base MSE:", mse.eval(y_pred=3, y_true=5))
print("L2 penalty:", l2.eval(w=2.0))     # 0.01 * 4 = 0.04

docs.title: Multi-Step Composition
docs.text:
Build complex pipelines step by step:

from neurogebra import Expression

# Step 1: Normalize input
normalize = Expression("normalize", "(x - mean) / std",
                       params={"mean": 0.0, "std": 1.0})

# Step 2: Linear transformation
linear = Expression("linear", "w * x + b",
                    params={"w": 1.0, "b": 0.0})

# Step 3: Activation
from neurogebra import MathForge
forge = MathForge()
relu = forge.get("relu")

# Chain them: relu(w * normalize(x) + b)
step1 = linear.compose(normalize)   # w * ((x-mean)/std) + b
final = relu.compose(step1)         # relu(above)

print(f"Pipeline: {final.symbolic_expr}")

docs.title: Practical Example: Custom Model
docs.text:
from neurogebra import Expression, MathForge
import numpy as np

forge = MathForge()

# Build a simple 2-layer network expression
# Layer 1: h = relu(w1*x + b1)
# Layer 2: y = w2*h + b2

# We can compose this step by step
layer1_linear = Expression("l1", "w1*x + b1",
                           params={"w1": 0.5, "b1": 0.0})

relu = forge.get("relu")
layer1 = relu.compose(layer1_linear)  # relu(w1*x + b1)

print(f"Layer 1 output at x=2: {layer1.eval(x=2)}")
# relu(0.5*2 + 0) = relu(1.0) = 1.0

docs.title: Tips for Composition
docs.text:
Best Practices

  1. Start simple — compose from well-tested building blocks
  2. Test each step — evaluate intermediate expressions
  3. Register reusable expressions — forge.register("name", expr)
  4. Use string composition for quick experiments — forge.compose("mse + 0.1*mae")
  5. Check gradients — composed expressions have gradients too!

Next: Training Expressions →

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text: NeuroGebra exposes 48 unique loader methods through CombinedDatasets: 21 base loaders and 27 expanded loaders. The complete catalog lists every method, options, return convention and provenance.

docs.title: Load a small teaching dataset
docs.text:
from neurogebra.datasets import Datasets

(X_train, y_train), (X_test, y_test) = Datasets.load_iris(verbose=False)
print(X_train.shape, y_train.shape)
print(X_test.shape, y_test.shape)

This loader generates Iris-like synthetic data; it does not return the original Iris dataset. Familiar names are teaching conveniences, so always check provenance before reporting a benchmark result.

docs.title: Handle pair-returning loaders
docs.text:
from neurogebra.datasets import Datasets

X, y = Datasets.load_digits(verbose=False)
split = int(0.8 * len(X))
X_train, X_test = X[:split], X[split:]
y_train, y_test = y[:split], y[split:]

This example illustrates unpacking. For evaluation, shuffle or stratify before splitting; the synthetic digits fallback groups examples by class. Fit preprocessing using only the training partition.

docs.title: Use the expanded generators
docs.text:
from neurogebra.datasets import CombinedDatasets

X, y = CombinedDatasets.load_checkerboard(n_samples=200, verbose=False)
print(X.shape, y.shape)

Expanded generators currently use NumPy's global RNG in several paths. For strict reproducibility, record seeds and isolate generation from training; conversion to local generator instances is tracked in the review.

docs.title: Original data and optional integrations
docs.text:
Wine, Breast Cancer, Digits, Diabetes and California Housing can use scikit-learn sources when available, with a synthetic fallback on failure. California Housing can require a download. The other loaders generate distributions locally. The datasets extra installs scikit-learn but does not replace every synthetic generator with original benchmark data.

For published results, use the original dataset publisher or an official framework loader, record the data license and preprocessing, and preserve an uncontaminated test set.

docs.title: Expressions — Building Blocks
docs.text: Create a formula, evaluate a batch, and derive its slope. An Expression stores a SymPy formula and parameters; tensor autograd and neural layers use separate execution paths.

docs.title: A complete first example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from neurogebra import Expression

square = Expression("square", "x**2")
x = np.array([-2.0, 0.0, 2.0])
print(square.eval(x=x))                 # [4. 0. 4.]
print(square.gradient("x").eval(x=x))   # [-4. 0. 4.]
print(square.latex())

Use named inputs such as x=.... Parameters belong in params; array inputs follow NumPy broadcasting. Inspect a formula's domain before evaluating logarithms, roots, or divisions. See the Expression reference.

docs.title: What is an Expression?
docs.text:
An Expression is a symbolic mathematical formula that can:

  • Evaluate — compute a numerical result
  • Differentiate — compute gradients symbolically
  • Explain — describe itself in plain English
  • Compose — combine with other expressions
  • Train — learn parameters from data
  • Visualize — plot itself

docs.title: Creating an Expression
docs.text:
from neurogebra import Expression

# Simple: name + formula
square = Expression("square", "x**2")

# With parameters
line = Expression("line", "m*x + b", params={"m": 2.0, "b": 1.0})

# With trainable parameters
trainable_line = Expression(
    "trainable_line",
    "m*x + b",
    params={"m": 0.0, "b": 0.0},
    trainable_params=["m", "b"]
)

# With metadata
custom = Expression(
    "my_function",
    "x * tanh(x)",
    metadata={
        "category": "activation",
        "description": "Custom activation function",
        "usage": "Experimental hidden layers"
    }
)

docs.title: With Keyword Arguments
docs.text:
expr = Expression("poly", "a*x**2 + b*x + c",
                  params={"a": 1.0, "b": -2.0, "c": 1.0})

# Parameters are substituted automatically
result = expr.eval(x=3)
print(result)  # 1*9 + (-2)*3 + 1 = 4.0

docs.title: With NumPy Arrays
docs.text:
import numpy as np

square = Expression("square", "x**2")
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
result = square.eval(x=x)
print(result)  # [ 1  4  9 16 25]

docs.title: Expression with Multiple Variables
docs.text:
loss = Expression("mse", "(y_pred - y_true)**2")
result = loss.eval(y_pred=3.0, y_true=5.0)
print(result)  # 4.0

docs.title: Expression Properties
docs.text:
from neurogebra import MathForge

forge = MathForge()
sigmoid = forge.get("sigmoid")

# Name
print(sigmoid.name)             # "sigmoid"

# Symbolic formula (SymPy expression)
print(sigmoid.symbolic_expr)    # 1/(1 + exp(-x))

# Variables (free symbols)
print(sigmoid.variables)        # [x]

# Parameters
print(sigmoid.params)           # {}

# Metadata
print(sigmoid.metadata)
# {'category': 'activation', 'description': '...', ...}

docs.title: Explaining Expressions
docs.text:
Every expression can explain itself:

relu = forge.get("relu")
print(relu.explain())

sigmoid = forge.get("sigmoid")
print(sigmoid.explain())

# Metadata gives you detailed info
print(sigmoid.metadata["description"])
print(sigmoid.metadata["usage"])
print(sigmoid.metadata["pros"])
print(sigmoid.metadata["cons"])

docs.title: Expression Arithmetic
docs.text:
Expressions support standard math operations:

from neurogebra import Expression

a = Expression("a", "x**2")
b = Expression("b", "x + 1")

# Addition
c = a + b           # x² + x + 1

# Subtraction
d = a - b           # x² - x - 1

# Multiplication
e = a * b           # x² * (x + 1) = x³ + x²

# Scalar multiplication
f = 2 * a           # 2x²
g = a * 0.5         # 0.5x²

docs.title: Cloning Expressions
docs.text:
Create independent copies:

original = forge.get("relu")
clone = original.clone()

# Modifying clone doesn't affect original
clone.params["new_param"] = 42
print("new_param" in original.params)  # False

docs.title: Calling Expressions
docs.text:
Expressions are callable (you can use them like functions):

relu = forge.get("relu")

# These are equivalent:
result1 = relu.eval(x=5)
result2 = relu(5)
print(result1, result2)  # 5, 5

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
from neurogebra import Expression, MathForge
import numpy as np

# === Create Custom Expression ===
gaussian = Expression(
    "gaussian",
    "exp(-x**2 / (2 * sigma**2))",
    params={"sigma": 1.0},
    metadata={
        "category": "statistics",
        "description": "Gaussian (bell curve) function"
    }
)

# === Evaluate ===
x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 7)
y = gaussian.eval(x=x)
print("Gaussian values:")
for xi, yi in zip(x, y):
    print(f"  x={xi:+.1f}  →  f(x)={yi:.4f}")

# === Gradient ===
grad = gaussian.gradient("x")
print(f"\nGradient formula: {grad.symbolic_expr}")

# === Change parameter ===
gaussian.params["sigma"] = 0.5  # Narrower bell curve
y_narrow = gaussian.eval(x=x)
print("\nNarrower Gaussian:")
for xi, yi in zip(x, y_narrow):
    print(f"  x={xi:+.1f}  →  f(x)={yi:.4f}")

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
Property/Method Description Example .name Expression name "relu" .symbolic_expr SymPy formula Max(0, x) .variables Free variables [x] .params Parameter dict {"alpha": 0.01} .metadata Extra info {"category": "activation"} .eval(**kwargs) Evaluate numerically .eval(x=5) .gradient(var) Symbolic derivative .gradient("x") .compose(other) Compose: self(other) .compose(linear) .clone() Deep copy .clone() .explain() Plain English explanation .explain() .visualize() Plot the expression .visualize()

Next: Activation Functions →

docs.title: Gradients & Differentiation
docs.text: Gradients are how neural networks learn. This is the single most important concept in all of ML.

docs.title: The Big Picture
docs.text:
Training a neural network is just this:

  1. Make a prediction
  2. Measure the error (loss)
  3. Compute gradients — how much does each parameter affect the error?
  4. Adjust parameters in the direction that reduces error
  5. Repeat

Step 3 is what this page is about.

docs.title: What is a Gradient?
docs.text:
A gradient (derivative) tells you: if I change this input a tiny bit, how much does the output change?

\[f(x) = x^2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad f'(x) = 2x\]

At \(x = 3\): \(f'(3) = 6\), meaning the output changes ~6 times faster than the input at that point.

docs.title: Symbolic Gradients in Neurogebra
docs.text:
Neurogebra computes gradients symbolically — you get the actual derivative formula, not just a number:

from neurogebra import Expression

# Define a function
f = Expression("quadratic", "x**2 + 3*x + 2")

# Compute its derivative
f_prime = f.gradient("x")

# See the formula
print(f"f(x) = {f.symbolic_expr}")       # x**2 + 3*x + 2
print(f"f'(x) = {f_prime.symbolic_expr}")  # 2*x + 3

# Evaluate at specific points
print(f"f'(0) = {f_prime.eval(x=0)}")    # 3
print(f"f'(1) = {f_prime.eval(x=1)}")    # 5
print(f"f'(-1) = {f_prime.eval(x=-1)}")  # 1

docs.title: Gradients of Activation Functions
docs.text:
from neurogebra import MathForge

forge = MathForge()

# ReLU gradient
relu = forge.get("relu")
relu_grad = relu.gradient("x")
print(f"ReLU'(x) = {relu_grad.symbolic_expr}")
# Derivative is 1 for x > 0, 0 for x < 0

# Sigmoid gradient
sigmoid = forge.get("sigmoid")
sig_grad = sigmoid.gradient("x")
print(f"Sigmoid'(x) = {sig_grad.symbolic_expr}")
# σ'(x) = σ(x) · (1 - σ(x))

# Tanh gradient
tanh = forge.get("tanh")
tanh_grad = tanh.gradient("x")
print(f"Tanh'(x) = {tanh_grad.symbolic_expr}")
# tanh'(x) = 1 - tanh²(x)

docs.title: Gradients of Loss Functions
docs.text:
This is directly used in training:

mse = forge.get("mse")
print(f"MSE = {mse.symbolic_expr}")
# (y_pred - y_true)**2

mse_grad = mse.gradient("y_pred")
print(f"dMSE/d(y_pred) = {mse_grad.symbolic_expr}")
# 2*(y_pred - y_true)

# Interpretation:
# If prediction > target → gradient is positive → decrease prediction
# If prediction < target → gradient is negative → increase prediction
print(f"  pred=7, true=5: grad = {mse_grad.eval(y_pred=7, y_true=5)}")  # 4
print(f"  pred=3, true=5: grad = {mse_grad.eval(y_pred=3, y_true=5)}")  # -4
print(f"  pred=5, true=5: grad = {mse_grad.eval(y_pred=5, y_true=5)}")  # 0 (perfect!)

docs.title: Higher-Order Derivatives
docs.text:
You can differentiate multiple times:

f = Expression("cubic", "x**3")

f1 = f.gradient("x")     # First derivative
f2 = f1.gradient("x")    # Second derivative
f3 = f2.gradient("x")    # Third derivative

print(f"f(x)    = {f.symbolic_expr}")    # x³
print(f"f'(x)   = {f1.symbolic_expr}")   # 3x²
print(f"f''(x)  = {f2.symbolic_expr}")   # 6x
print(f"f'''(x) = {f3.symbolic_expr}")   # 6

docs.title: Partial Derivatives
docs.text:
For functions with multiple variables:

# f(x, y) = x²y + xy²
f = Expression("multi", "x**2*y + x*y**2")

# Partial derivative with respect to x
df_dx = f.gradient("x")
print(f"∂f/∂x = {df_dx.symbolic_expr}")  # 2*x*y + y²

# Partial derivative with respect to y
df_dy = f.gradient("y")
print(f"∂f/∂y = {df_dy.symbolic_expr}")  # x² + 2*x*y

docs.title: Gradient Descent — Using Gradients to Learn
docs.text:
Here's a manual gradient descent implementation to see how gradients drive learning:

import numpy as np
from neurogebra import Expression

# Goal: Find x that minimizes f(x) = (x - 3)²
# Answer should be x = 3

f = Expression("parabola", "(x - 3)**2")
f_grad = f.gradient("x")  # f'(x) = 2*(x-3)

# Gradient descent
x = 10.0          # Start far from minimum
lr = 0.1          # Learning rate

print(f"{'Step':>4} | {'x':>8} | {'f(x)':>8} | {'gradient':>8}")
print("-" * 45)

for step in range(15):
    fx = f.eval(x=x)
    gx = f_grad.eval(x=x)

    print(f"{step:>4} | {x:>8.4f} | {fx:>8.4f} | {gx:>8.4f}")

    # Update: move opposite to gradient
    x = x - lr * gx

print(f"\nFinal x = {x:.4f}")  # Should be close to 3.0

docs.title: The Vanishing Gradient Problem
docs.text:
Some activations have gradients that become very small, making learning slow or impossible:

import numpy as np

forge = MathForge()

# Sigmoid gradient becomes tiny for large |x|
sig_grad = forge.get("sigmoid").gradient("x")
for x_val in [-10, -5, 0, 5, 10]:
    g = sig_grad.eval(x=x_val)
    print(f"  sigmoid'({x_val:>3}) = {g:.6f}")

# Output:
# sigmoid'(-10) = 0.000045  ← Almost zero! Learning stops.
# sigmoid'( -5) = 0.006648
# sigmoid'(  0) = 0.250000  ← OK
# sigmoid'(  5) = 0.006648
# sigmoid'( 10) = 0.000045  ← Almost zero!

print("\nReLU doesn't have this problem:")
relu_grad = forge.get("relu").gradient("x")
for x_val in [-10, -5, 0, 5, 10]:
    g = relu_grad.eval(x=x_val)
    print(f"  relu'({x_val:>3}) = {g}")

Why this matters

The vanishing gradient problem is why ReLU replaced Sigmoid as the default activation for hidden layers. With Sigmoid, deep networks couldn't learn because gradients became too small.

docs.title: Numerical Gradients (Finite Differences)
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to verify symbolic gradients using numerical approximation:

def numerical_gradient(expr, var_name, point, epsilon=1e-5):
    """Compute gradient numerically using finite differences."""
    kwargs_plus = {var_name: point + epsilon}
    kwargs_minus = {var_name: point - epsilon}
    return (expr.eval(**kwargs_plus) - expr.eval(**kwargs_minus)) / (2 * epsilon)

f = Expression("test", "x**3 + 2*x + 1")
f_grad = f.gradient("x")

x_point = 2.0
symbolic = f_grad.eval(x=x_point)
numerical = numerical_gradient(f, "x", x_point)

print(f"Symbolic gradient:  {symbolic:.6f}")   # 14.000000
print(f"Numerical gradient: {numerical:.6f}")  # 14.000000
print(f"Difference: {abs(symbolic - numerical):.10f}")  # ~0

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Concept What It Is Why It Matters Gradient Rate of change Tells model how to adjust Positive gradient Output increases with input Decrease the parameter Negative gradient Output decreases with input Increase the parameter Zero gradient At a minimum/maximum Training converged (maybe) Vanishing gradient Gradient too small Model stops learning Exploding gradient Gradient too large Training becomes unstable

Next: Expression Composition →

docs.title: Loss Functions
docs.text: A loss function measures how wrong your model's predictions are. The goal of training is to minimize the loss.

docs.title: The Concept
docs.text:
Model Prediction: ŷ = 4.5
Actual Value:     y  = 5.0

Loss = some_function(ŷ, y)
      = how_wrong_is_the_prediction

If loss is high → model is bad → adjust weights
If loss is low  → model is good → we're done (or close)

docs.title: Exploring Loss Functions
docs.text:
from neurogebra import MathForge

forge = MathForge()
losses = forge.list_all(category="loss")
print(losses)
# ['mse', 'mae', 'binary_crossentropy', 'huber', 'log_cosh', 'hinge', ...]

docs.title: MSE — Mean Squared Error
docs.text:
The most common loss for regression tasks.

\[\text{MSE} = (y_{pred} - y_{true})^2\] 
mse = forge.get("mse")

# Close prediction → small loss
print(mse.eval(y_pred=4.8, y_true=5.0))  # 0.04

# Bad prediction → large loss
print(mse.eval(y_pred=2.0, y_true=5.0))  # 9.0

# Perfect prediction → zero loss
print(mse.eval(y_pred=5.0, y_true=5.0))  # 0.0

Properties:

  • Squares the error → penalizes large errors heavily
  • Always non-negative
  • Smooth and differentiable → nice gradients
# The gradient tells the model HOW to adjust
grad = mse.gradient("y_pred")
print(grad.symbolic_expr)  # 2*(y_pred - y_true)
# If pred > true: gradient is positive → decrease prediction
# If pred < true: gradient is negative → increase prediction

When to use MSE

Regression tasks. Best when outliers are rare and you want to penalize large errors.

docs.title: MAE — Mean Absolute Error
docs.text:
More robust to outliers than MSE.

\[\text{MAE} = |y_{pred} - y_{true}|\] 
mae = forge.get("mae")

print(mae.eval(y_pred=4.8, y_true=5.0))  # 0.2
print(mae.eval(y_pred=2.0, y_true=5.0))  # 3.0
print(mae.eval(y_pred=5.0, y_true=5.0))  # 0.0

MSE vs MAE:

Error MSE MAE Small (0.2) 0.04 0.2 Medium (3.0) 9.0 3.0 Large (10.0) 100.0 10.0

MSE squares errors, so it punishes outliers much more. MAE treats all errors linearly.

When to use MAE

Regression with outliers. More robust than MSE but converges slower.

docs.title: Binary Cross-Entropy
docs.text:
The standard loss for binary classification (yes/no problems).

\[\text{BCE} = -[y_{true} \cdot \log(y_{pred}) + (1-y_{true}) \cdot \log(1-y_{pred})]\] 
bce = forge.get("binary_crossentropy")

# Model says 0.9 probability, actual is 1 (correct!) → low loss
print(bce.eval(y_pred=0.9, y_true=1.0))  # ≈ 0.105

# Model says 0.1 probability, actual is 1 (wrong!) → high loss
print(bce.eval(y_pred=0.1, y_true=1.0))  # ≈ 2.303

# Model says 0.9, actual is 0 (wrong!) → high loss
print(bce.eval(y_pred=0.9, y_true=0.0))  # ≈ 2.303

When to use Binary Cross-Entropy

Binary classification (spam/not-spam, disease/healthy). Always pair with sigmoid output.

docs.title: Huber Loss
docs.text:
Best of both worlds — MSE for small errors, MAE for large errors.

\[L_\delta = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}(y_{pred} - y_{true})^2 & \text{if } |y_{pred} - y_{true}| \leq \delta \\ \delta|y_{pred} - y_{true}| - \frac{1}{2}\delta^2 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\] 
huber = forge.get("huber")

# Small error → behaves like MSE (smooth)
# Large error → behaves like MAE (robust)
print(huber.eval(y_pred=4.8, y_true=5.0))  # ≈ 0.02 (MSE-like)
print(huber.eval(y_pred=0.0, y_true=5.0))  # ≈ 4.5  (MAE-like, not 25!)

When to use Huber

Regression with occasional outliers. Great balance between MSE and MAE. Popular in reinforcement learning.

docs.title: Hinge Loss
docs.text:
For SVM-style classification with margin.

\[L = \max(0, 1 - y_{true} \cdot y_{pred})\] 
hinge = forge.get("hinge")

# Correct with margin → zero loss
print(hinge.eval(y_pred=2.0, y_true=1.0))   # 0 (correct & confident)

# Correct but no margin → some loss
print(hinge.eval(y_pred=0.5, y_true=1.0))  # 0.5

# Wrong → high loss
print(hinge.eval(y_pred=-1.0, y_true=1.0))  # 2.0

docs.title: Log-Cosh Loss
docs.text:
Smooth alternative to Huber Loss.

\[L = \log(\cosh(y_{pred} - y_{true}))\] 
log_cosh = forge.get("log_cosh")

print(log_cosh.eval(y_pred=4.8, y_true=5.0))  # ≈ 0.020
print(log_cosh.eval(y_pred=0.0, y_true=5.0))  # ≈ 4.307

docs.title: Choosing the Right Loss Function
docs.text:
What's your task?
│
├── REGRESSION (predicting a number)
│   ├── No outliers       → MSE
│   ├── Has outliers      → MAE or Huber
│   └── Smooth & robust   → Log-Cosh
│
├── BINARY CLASSIFICATION (yes/no)
│   └── → Binary Cross-Entropy + Sigmoid
│
├── MULTI-CLASS CLASSIFICATION (cat/dog/bird)
│   └── → Cross-Entropy + Softmax
│
└── MARGIN-BASED (SVM-style)
    └── → Hinge Loss

docs.title: Comparing Loss Functions
docs.text:
from neurogebra import MathForge
import numpy as np

forge = MathForge()

# Different error levels
errors = [0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0]

print(f"{'Error':>6} | {'MSE':>8} | {'MAE':>8} | {'Huber':>8}")
print("-" * 40)

for err in errors:
    mse_val = forge.get("mse").eval(y_pred=err, y_true=0)
    mae_val = forge.get("mae").eval(y_pred=err, y_true=0)
    # Huber needs delta param
    huber_val = min(0.5 * err**2, abs(err) - 0.5)  # delta=1

    print(f"{err:>6.1f} | {mse_val:>8.3f} | {mae_val:>8.3f} | {huber_val:>8.3f}")

docs.title: Composing Custom Losses
docs.text:
# Weighted combination
hybrid = forge.compose("mse + 0.1*mae")

# Evaluate
result = hybrid.eval(y_pred=3.0, y_true=5.0)
print(f"Hybrid loss: {result}")

docs.text:

  2. Which loss function is most sensitive to the error (pred=0, true=10)?

docs.title: MathForge — The Core
docs.text: MathForge is the central hub of Neurogebra. It's the first thing you create and the main way you interact with the library.

docs.title: What is MathForge?
docs.text:
MathForge is a repository manager that gives you access to 285 pre-built mathematical expressions used in Machine Learning and scientific computing.

Think of it as a library catalog — you ask for a book (expression) by name, and it gives you a full object you can work with.

docs.title: Creating MathForge
docs.text:
from neurogebra import MathForge

forge = MathForge()

When you create a MathForge, it automatically loads all expressions from these categories:

  • Activations (ReLU, Sigmoid, Tanh, etc.)
  • Losses (MSE, MAE, Cross-Entropy, etc.)
  • Regularizers (L1, L2, Elastic Net)
  • Algebra (Polynomial, Quadratic, etc.)
  • Calculus (Derivative-related expressions)
  • Statistics (Mean, Variance, etc.)
  • Linear Algebra (Dot product, Norms, etc.)
  • Metrics (Accuracy, Precision, etc.)
  • Optimization (Gradient descent steps)
  • Transforms (Normalization, Standardization)

docs.title: Basic Get
docs.text:
# Get by name
relu = forge.get("relu")
sigmoid = forge.get("sigmoid")
mse = forge.get("mse")

docs.title: Get with Custom Parameters
docs.text:
# Leaky ReLU has an 'alpha' parameter (default 0.01)
leaky = forge.get("leaky_relu")
print(leaky.params)  # {'alpha': 0.01}

# Override it
leaky_custom = forge.get("leaky_relu", params={"alpha": 0.2})
print(leaky_custom.params)  # {'alpha': 0.2}

docs.title: Get as Trainable
docs.text:
# Make all parameters trainable
trainable_expr = forge.get("leaky_relu", trainable=True)
# Now 'alpha' can be learned from data

docs.title: List Everything
docs.text:
all_exprs = forge.list_all()
print(f"Total expressions: {len(all_exprs)}")
print(all_exprs)

docs.title: List by Category
docs.text:
# Activation functions
activations = forge.list_all(category="activation")
print("Activations:", activations)

# Loss functions
losses = forge.list_all(category="loss")
print("Losses:", losses)

# Regularizers
regularizers = forge.list_all(category="regularizer")
print("Regularizers:", regularizers)

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
Don't know the exact name? Search for it:

# Search by keyword
results = forge.search("smooth")
print(results)

results = forge.search("classification")
print(results)

results = forge.search("gradient")
print(results)

docs.title: Composing Expressions
docs.text:
Combine expressions using string notation:

# Custom loss = MSE + 0.1 * MAE
hybrid_loss = forge.compose("mse + 0.1*mae")

# Evaluate the composed expression
result = hybrid_loss.eval(y_pred=3.0, y_true=5.0)
print(f"Hybrid loss: {result}")

docs.title: Registering Custom Expressions
docs.text:
You can add your own expressions to the forge:

from neurogebra import Expression

# Create a custom expression
my_func = Expression(
    "my_activation",
    "x * tanh(x)",
    metadata={"category": "activation", "description": "x*tanh(x) activation"}
)

# Register it
forge.register("my_activation", my_func)

# Now you can get it like any built-in expression
retrieved = forge.get("my_activation")
print(retrieved.eval(x=2.0))

docs.title: Complete Example
docs.text:
from neurogebra import MathForge

forge = MathForge()

# 1. Explore what's available
print("=== Available Categories ===")
for category in ["activation", "loss", "regularizer"]:
    exprs = forge.list_all(category=category)
    print(f"  {category}: {len(exprs)} expressions")

# 2. Get and explore an expression
print("\n=== Sigmoid ===")
sigmoid = forge.get("sigmoid")
print(f"  Formula: {sigmoid.symbolic_expr}")
print(f"  sigmoid(0) = {sigmoid.eval(x=0)}")
print(f"  sigmoid(5) = {sigmoid.eval(x=5):.4f}")

# 3. Compare activations
print("\n=== Activation Comparison at x=1.0 ===")
for name in ["relu", "sigmoid", "tanh", "swish", "gelu"]:
    expr = forge.get(name)
    val = expr.eval(x=1.0)
    print(f"  {name:>10}: {val:.4f}")

# 4. Compose a hybrid loss
print("\n=== Hybrid Loss ===")
loss = forge.compose("mse + 0.1*mae")
error = loss.eval(y_pred=2.5, y_true=3.0)
print(f"  Loss value: {error:.4f}")

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
Method Description Example forge.get(name) Get expression by name forge.get("relu") forge.get(name, params={}) Get with custom params forge.get("leaky_relu", params={"alpha": 0.2}) forge.list_all() List all expressions forge.list_all() forge.list_all(category=) List by category forge.list_all(category="activation") forge.search(query) Search expressions forge.search("smooth") forge.compose(str) Compose from string forge.compose("mse + 0.1*mae") forge.register(name, expr) Add custom expression forge.register("my_fn", expr)

docs.title: ModelBuilder
docs.text: Construct a sequential neural network, train it with NumPy, and inspect its predictions. Dense inputs use (samples, features); image layers use NHWC.

docs.title: A complete first example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from neurogebra import ModelBuilder

builder = ModelBuilder()
model = builder.Sequential([builder.Dense(1)], name="line")
X = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 32).reshape(-1, 1)
y = 2.0 * X + 1.0
model.compile(loss="mse", optimizer="sgd", learning_rate=0.05)
history = model.fit(X, y, epochs=5, batch_size=32,
                    validation_split=0, verbose=False)
print(len(history["loss"]))        # 5
print(model.predict(X[:2]).shape)  # (2, 1)

Weights initialize on the first forward pass. Exact losses depend on initialization and data order; a short example is not a convergence guarantee. Use a single output with MSE for this regression task. See optimizers, datasets, and the builders reference.

docs.title: What is ModelBuilder?
docs.text:
ModelBuilder lets you:

  • Build neural networks layer by layer
  • Understand what each layer does
  • Get explanations and best-practice suggestions
  • Use pre-built templates for common tasks

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
from neurogebra import ModelBuilder

builder = ModelBuilder()

# Build a simple classifier
model = builder.Sequential([
    builder.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
    builder.Dropout(0.2),
    builder.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    builder.Dense(10, activation="softmax")
])

# See what you built
model.summary()

docs.title: Dense (Fully Connected)
docs.text:
Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer.

# Basic dense layer
layer = builder.Dense(128, activation="relu")

# With input shape (first layer only)
first_layer = builder.Dense(128, activation="relu", input_shape=(784,))

# Learn what it does
layer.explain()

Output of explain(): 

 DENSE Layer
   Fully connected layer - every neuron connects to every neuron in next layer

   Best used for:
   • Classification
   • Regression
   • Final output layer

   Neurons/Units: 128
   Activation: relu

docs.title: Dropout
docs.text:
Randomly deactivates neurons during training to prevent overfitting.

dropout = builder.Dropout(rate=0.2)  # Drop 20% of neurons
dropout.explain()

docs.title: Conv2D (Convolutional)
docs.text:
Detects patterns in images using sliding filters.

conv = builder.Conv2D(filters=32, kernel_size=3, activation="relu")
conv.explain()

docs.title: MaxPooling2D
docs.text:
Reduces image dimensions by taking maximum values in regions.

pool = builder.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2)
pool.explain()

docs.title: Flatten
docs.text:
Converts multi-dimensional data to 1D for dense layers.

flatten = builder.Flatten()

docs.title: BatchNorm
docs.text:
Normalizes layer outputs across the batch to stabilize training.

bn = builder.BatchNorm()
bn.explain()

docs.title: LayerNorm
docs.text:
Normalizes activations across feature dimensions for each individual sample, crucial for deep transformers and residual architectures.

ln = builder.LayerNorm(eps=1e-5)

docs.title: GlobalAveragePooling2D
docs.text:
Reduces spatial feature maps \((B, H, W, C) \to (B, C)\) by averaging across all spatial pixels, drastically reducing parameter count compared to Flatten.

gap = builder.GlobalAveragePooling2D()

docs.title: ResidualDense
docs.text:
Implements an identity shortcut skip-connection \((x + \text{Dense}(x))\) that mitigates vanishing gradients and allows very deep MLP/ResNet networks to train effectively.

res_block = builder.ResidualDense(units=64, activation="relu")

docs.title: Sequential Model
docs.text:
Layers stacked one after another:

# Simple classifier
classifier = builder.Sequential([
    builder.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
    builder.Dropout(0.2),
    builder.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    builder.Dense(10, activation="softmax")
], name="my_classifier")

classifier.summary()

docs.title: From Template
docs.text:
Use pre-built architectures:

# See available templates
builder.list_templates()

# Create from template
model = builder.from_template("simple_classifier")
model.summary()

# Other templates:
# - "simple_classifier"  → Basic dense network
# - "image_classifier"   → CNN for images
# - "regression"         → For predicting numbers
# - "binary_classifier"  → For yes/no tasks

docs.title: Simple Classifier
docs.text:
model = builder.from_template("simple_classifier")
model.explain_architecture()

Architecture: 

Dense(128, relu) → Dropout(0.2) → Dense(64, relu) → Dense(10, softmax)

docs.title: Image Classifier (CNN)
docs.text:
model = builder.from_template("image_classifier")
model.explain_architecture()

Architecture: 

Conv2D(32) → MaxPool → Conv2D(64) → MaxPool → Flatten → Dense(128) → Dense(10)

docs.title: Regression Network
docs.text:
model = builder.from_template("regression")

Architecture: 

Dense(64, relu) → Dense(32, relu) → Dense(1, linear)

docs.title: Binary Classifier
docs.text:
model = builder.from_template("binary_classifier")

Architecture: 

Dense(64, relu) → Dropout(0.3) → Dense(32, relu) → Dense(1, sigmoid)

docs.title: Architecture Suggestions
docs.text:
ModelBuilder can suggest architectures based on your task:

# Get suggestion for a task
builder.suggest_architecture(
    task="classification",
    input_size=784,
    output_size=10
)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
model.summary()

Shows the layer structure with types, units, and activations.

docs.title: Explain Architecture
docs.text:
model.explain_architecture()

Gives plain-English explanation of what each layer does and why it's there.

docs.title: Building an Image Classifier Step by Step
docs.text:
from neurogebra import ModelBuilder

builder = ModelBuilder()

# Step 1: Feature extraction (convolutions)
# Step 2: Dimensionality reduction (pooling)
# Step 3: Classification (dense layers)

model = builder.Sequential([
    # Feature extraction
    builder.Conv2D(32, kernel_size=3, activation="relu"),
    builder.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2),
    builder.Conv2D(64, kernel_size=3, activation="relu"),
    builder.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=2),

    # Bridge
    builder.Flatten(),

    # Classification
    builder.Dense(128, activation="relu"),
    builder.Dropout(0.5),
    builder.Dense(10, activation="softmax")
], name="mnist_classifier")

# Understand it
model.summary()
model.explain_architecture()

docs.title: Layer Selection Guide
docs.text: Task Layers to Use Tabular data classification Dense → Dropout → Dense → Softmax Image classification Conv2D → MaxPool → Dense → Softmax Binary classification Dense → Dense → Dense(1) → Sigmoid Regression Dense → Dense → Dense(1) → Linear Layer When to Use Dense Always (at least for the output) Dropout When you have overfitting Conv2D For images/spatial data MaxPooling2D After Conv2D to reduce size Flatten Between Conv and Dense BatchNorm For deeper networks to stabilize training LayerNorm Per-sample feature normalization for deep ResNets/transformers GlobalAveragePooling2D Extreme parameter reduction before final classification ResidualDense Residual skip-connection for deep MLP architectures

docs.title: Saving and Loading Models
docs.text:
from neurogebra.builders.model_builder import Model

# Save trained weights and architecture to disk
model.save("my_model.json")

# Restore model
loaded_model = Model.load("my_model.json")
predictions = loaded_model.predict(X_test)

docs.title: Step-by-Step Batch Training
docs.text:
For customized training loops or active learning:

# Train single mini-batch
batch_metrics = model.train_on_batch(X_batch, y_batch)
print(f"Batch Loss: {batch_metrics['loss']:.4f}")

docs.title: Tensors
docs.text: Use multidimensional NumPy-backed arrays with gradient tracking. This guide connects array operations, shapes and reverse-mode derivatives.

docs.title: A complete first example
docs.text:
from neurogebra.core.autograd import Tensor

x = Tensor([[1.0, 2.0]], requires_grad=True)
loss = (x * x).sum()
loss.backward()
print(x.shape)  # (1, 2)
print(x.grad)   # [[2. 4.]]

The sum produces a scalar objective; its gradient has the same shape as x. Leaf gradients accumulate across backward calls. Rebuild the forward graph after updates, and do not mutate input storage before backward. See the Tensor reference.

docs.title: What is a Tensor?
docs.text:
A tensor is a multi-dimensional array with automatic gradient tracking:

  • Scalar (0D tensor): 42
  • Vector (1D tensor): [1, 2, 3]
  • Matrix (2D tensor): [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
  • 3D tensor: A batch of matrices

docs.title: Creating Tensors
docs.text:
from neurogebra.core.autograd import Tensor

# From a list
t = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
print(t)        # Tensor(shape=(3,), requires_grad=False)
print(t.data)   # [1. 2. 3.]

# With gradient tracking enabled
t = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
print(t)        # Tensor(shape=(3,), requires_grad=True)
print(t.grad)   # [0. 0. 0.] — initialized to zeros

# 2D tensor
m = Tensor([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], requires_grad=True)
print(m.shape)  # (2, 2)
print(m.ndim)   # 2

docs.title: Tensor Properties
docs.text:
t = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)

print(t.shape)          # (3,)
print(t.ndim)           # 1
print(t.data)           # [1. 2. 3.]
print(t.grad)           # [0. 0. 0.]
print(t.requires_grad)  # True

docs.title: Element-wise Arithmetic
docs.text:
a = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)
b = Tensor([4.0, 5.0, 6.0], requires_grad=True)

c = a + b              # [5.0, 7.0, 9.0]
d = a * b              # [4.0, 10.0, 18.0]
e = a - b              # [-3.0, -3.0, -3.0]
f = a ** 2             # [1.0, 4.0, 9.0]

print(f"a + b = {c.data}")
print(f"a * b = {d.data}")
print(f"a ** 2 = {f.data}")

docs.title: Reduction Operations
docs.text:
a = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0], requires_grad=True)

s = a.sum()     # Sum of all elements → 10.0
m = a.mean()    # Mean of all elements → 2.5

print(f"sum = {s.data}")   # 10.0
print(f"mean = {m.data}")  # 2.5

docs.title: Backward Pass with Tensors
docs.text:
from neurogebra.core.autograd import Tensor

# Create tensor with gradient tracking
x = Tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)

# Computation: y = sum(x²) = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14
y = (x ** 2).sum()

# Backward pass
y.backward()

print(f"x = {x.data}")       # [1. 2. 3.]
print(f"y = x² sum = {y.data}")  # 14.0
print(f"dy/dx = {x.grad}")   # [2. 4. 6.] — which is 2*x

docs.title: Practical Example: Batch MSE Loss
docs.text:
from neurogebra.core.autograd import Tensor

# Predictions and targets (batch of 4)
predictions = Tensor([2.5, 0.1, 3.0, 7.0], requires_grad=True)
targets = Tensor([3.0, 0.0, 2.5, 8.0])

# MSE = mean((pred - target)²)
diff = predictions - targets
squared = diff ** 2
loss = squared.mean()

print(f"Predictions: {predictions.data}")
print(f"Targets:     {targets.data}")
print(f"MSE Loss:    {loss.data:.4f}")

# Backpropagate
loss.backward()
print(f"Gradients:   {predictions.grad}")
# Each gradient = 2*(pred-target)/n

docs.title: Zeroing Gradients
docs.text:
Always zero gradients between training iterations:

x = Tensor([1.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)

# First iteration
y = (x ** 2).sum()
y.backward()
print(f"After 1st backward: grad = {x.grad}")  # [2. 4.]

# Zero and compute again
x.zero_grad()
y = (x ** 2).sum()
y.backward()
print(f"After zero + 2nd backward: grad = {x.grad}")  # [2. 4.] — correct

docs.title: Key Differences: Value vs Tensor
docs.text:
Feature Value Tensor Data type Single float NumPy array Shape Scalar Any shape Use case Educational, simple networks Batched training Gradient Single float Array (same shape as data) Operations +, *, **, relu, sigmoid, tanh +, *, **, sum, mean
